blockers: Statute: OCR is established in the Department of Education Organization Act, and the earlier record cites the Congressional Research Service view that the Economy Act may not support transfers of statutory functions (not re-verified).

Congressional opposition: a 2026-09-30 letter from 139 organizations urges appropriators to block the move, and the FY2026 appropriations law (Pub. L. 119-75) limits ED fund transfers according to that letter; the Senate HELP amendment to bar the OCR move failed on 2026-07-30.
Capacity concerns raised by the National Center for Youth Law, school boards and others about DOJ handling OCR's complaint volume (over 23,000 complaints in FY2025, per K-12 Dive).
confidence_reason: ED's release was read and confirms the DOJ partnership and that OCR keeps its authorities within ED. Whether complaints are being referred to DOJ in practice rests on trade press through July 2026 and was not confirmed afterward; if referrals have begun, the stage would rise.

durability.why: The arrangement is a revocable interagency agreement and ED retains statutory authority.

est_completion.basis: Inference: the Mandate's version requires moving OCR by statute and limiting it to litigation, while the current arrangement keeps formal authority at ED, and the House bills did not include it.

proposal: The Mandate recommends moving the Office for Civil Rights to the Department of Justice, with the federal government enforcing civil rights through DOJ and the courts and OCR at DOJ enforcing only through litigation. It also suggests moving disability-discrimination enforcement assets from the special education office to DOJ.
remaining: Moving OCR itself, with its attorneys, to DOJ under statute; under the agreement ED retains formal authority over OCR.
Limiting DOJ-side enforcement to litigation: under the agreement DOJ investigates and recommends resolutions, while ED keeps mediation, settlements, guidance and administrative enforcement decisions.
Moving IDEA-related disability enforcement assets to DOJ: special education management is moving to HHS instead (see c11-03); ED retains IDEA enforcement authority.
Staffing, assets and workload division for the DOJ arrangement, which officials said in June 2026 would be worked out over the coming weeks; no later implementation report was found.

flags: operation of the DOJ agreement after July 2026 unverified
review.mandate_note: Page 330 says OCR should move to DOJ, with civil rights enforced through DOJ and the courts and OCR at DOJ enforcing only through litigation; page 327 says OSERS disability-discrimination enforcement assets should move to DOJ with OCR. The paraphrase is accurate.

significance.rationale: Moving OCR to DOJ with litigation-only enforcement changes how students' civil rights complaints are resolved.

status_summary: As of 2026-10-08 OCR remains part of ED, and the June 2026 arrangement with DOJ is announced but not shown to be operating at scale. ED's release (last-reviewed date 2026-06-16) announced agreements with the Department of Justice on civil rights enforcement, student privacy protection, and training and advisory services drawn from DOJ's school desegregation role; for civil rights enforcement it says the two agencies will combine capacities to evaluate, investigate and resolve civil rights complaints, that ED keeps all its statutory authorities and functions, and that enforcement continues without interruption. K-12 Dive and Littler, reading the agreement, report that OCR will refer complaints to DOJ's Civil Rights Division to evaluate, investigate and resolve, and may resolve complaints based on DOJ's proposed findings; the NWLC letter dates the civil rights agreement 2026-06-15. Education Week (2026-07-27) reports that OCR will reimburse DOJ for these services, that the agreement does not say whether staff will transfer, and that no referrals or counts had been reported. K-12 Dive reports ED keeps leadership of OCR, the choice between administrative enforcement and DOJ referral, mediation, settlements, guidance and the Civil Rights Data Collection; officials said staffing and workload division would be worked out over the coming weeks. A 2026-09-15 Government Executive report does not list OCR among offices being reassigned and says laid-off OCR staff were asked to return and attorneys are being hired, and a 2026-09-30 letter from 139 organizations says the administration has declared an intention to delegate OCR enforcement to DOJ. This differs from the Mandate's design of moving OCR itself to DOJ and limiting enforcement to litigation.

timeline.event: During the fall 2025 shutdown ED issues layoff notices to about 500 more employees, including in OCR; the notices were later rescinded (month only; day not given).
ED's November 2025 agreements leave civil rights enforcement at ED while it explores options.
GAO reports ED spent up to 38 million dollars on nine months of paid leave for OCR employees before reinstating them (February 2026; day not given).

ED announces agreements with DOJ on civil rights enforcement, student privacy protection, and training and advisory services (alongside an HHS agreement on special education). For civil rights enforcement, ED's release says the agencies will combine capacities to evaluate, investigate and resolve complaints, that ED keeps all its statutory authorities and functions, and that enforcement continues without interruption; the release gives no staffing statements and the agreement text was not retrieved. K-12 Dive reports OCR will refer complaints to DOJ to evaluate, investigate and resolve, and that ED keeps oversight, leads OCR and decides between administrative enforcement and DOJ referral; officials describe it as a first step with staffing to be worked out over the coming weeks.

Education Week reports OCR will refer complaints to DOJ's Civil Rights Division for evaluation, investigation and attempted resolution and will reimburse DOJ for the services; the agreement does not say whether staff or OCR's roughly $140 million budget will move to DOJ, no referrals or counts are reported, and DOJ declined to answer questions about enforcement choices. The article links a two-page joint ED and DOJ fact sheet.
In Senate HELP markup, a Democratic amendment to bar the civil rights office move to DOJ fails on a party-line vote; S. 5046, which names four other ED offices, advances 13-9 without covering OCR.

Government Executive reports OCR is not among the offices being reassigned, that laid-off OCR employees were asked to return after the Secretary acknowledged in April 2026 that some cuts went too far, and that OCR is hiring more attorneys.

The NWLC Action Fund, for 139 organizations, writes to House and Senate appropriators asking them to prevent moving OCR enforcement to DOJ under the interagency agreement dated 2026-06-15; the letter says the administration has declared an intention to delegate and does not state the move is complete.

title: Move the Office for Civil Rights to DOJ with litigation-only enforcement
uncertainties: The agreement text and the joint ED and DOJ fact sheet were not retrieved (the ed.gov agreement PDF returned HTTP 403 to an earlier researcher; ED's release gives no fact sheet URLs). ED's release was read through a fetch summary and has no printed release date; its last-reviewed date of 2026-06-16 matches the Education Week and K-12 Dive announcement date. The specific mechanics (referral of complaints, ED's retained choice of enforcement path, reimbursement) rest on K-12 Dive, Littler and Education Week, which read the agreement; ED's own release says only that the agencies combine capacities and that ED keeps its statutory authorities. No ED or DOJ release dated after 2026-06-16 on implementation was found, and no report of referrals in practice was found as of the Education Week piece of 2026-07-27. Sources differ on the signing date (June 15 per the NWLC letter, June 16 announcement). Which complaint types go to DOJ was not specified. Whether any OCR staff have been detailed to DOJ was not found. The 2025 OCR regional office closures and court cases over OCR layoffs were not researched by name. The Mandate's related recommendation to put OCR's Case Processing Manual through notice and comment (p. 357) was not checked. Month-only dates are approximate (first of month used). The stage stays proposed because the signed arrangement keeps statutory authority at ED and no operation of the referral process is documented; it could move to in_progress if referral or staff transfer is shown.
